{{Short description|Endless time or timelessness}}
{{Other uses}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=December 2015}}
{{Time sidebar}}

'''Eternity''', also '''sempiternity'''{{efn|Earliest / oldest extant source: 1599 <ref name="MWS"/>:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/sempiternity_n|title=sempiternity noun Factsheet|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref> "thy muse to sempiternity"<ref>{{cite book|author=Thomas Nashe|author-link=Thomas Nashe|date=1599|editor=Nina Green|url=http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf|title=Nashe's Lenten Stuff|page=16|publisher=oxford-shakespeare.com|archive-date=August 3, 2016|access-date=December 31, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160803185514/http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>}}<ref name="MWS">{{cite web|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/sempiternity|title=sempiternity noun|publisher=[[Merriam-Webster]]}}</ref> or '''forever''',{{efn|in the context of [[future]] only - also '''everlasting'''}} or '''perpetuity''',<ref>{{Cite Merriam-Webster|eternity|access-date=2026-06-06}}</ref> is [[time]] with no [[:wikt:end#English|end]]<ref>{{cite web|author=[[Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary|Cambridge Dictionary]]|url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/eternity|title=
Meaning of eternity in English|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]}}</ref> i.e. [[Infinity|infinite]].<ref>{{cite web|author=[[dictionary.com]]|url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/eternity|title=American eternity|publisher=IXL Learning}}</ref> 

In the context of human life, eternity and [[death]] are co-existing realities.<ref>{{cite book|author=Noah Webster|author-link=Noah Webster|date=1856|title=A Dictionary of the English Language Exhibiting the Origin, Orthography, Pronunciation and Definitions of Words|chapter=ETH EUD|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HCjzHOKhqNoC&dq=eternity+etymology+death&pg=PA369|page=369|publisher=[[George Routledge]] & Company|quote=Eternity the state or time after death: as, at death we enter on ''eternity''}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Irene Sibbing-Plantholt|location=[[Freie Universität Berlin|Freie Universität]] [[Berlin]]/[[Einstein Foundation Berlin|Einstein Center Chronoi]]|editor=Anne Blankenship|date=6 October 2021|url=https://compass.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/rec3.12420|title=Coping with time and death in the Ancient Near East|journal=[[Religious Compass]]|volume=15|issue=11|article-number=e12420 |doi=10.1111/rec3.12420|issn=1749-8171|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons Ltd]]|quote=All humans, past and future, are forced to grapple with the abstract phenomenon of passing and ending time, as well as ideas about time, such as eternity and finality. Death especially is a confrontation with the passing, ending, irreversibility, and unpredictability of time,|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Lowell Gustfson|location=[[Villanova University]]|editor1=Lowell Gustafson|editor2=Barry Rodrigue|editor3=David Blanks|date=5 July 2022|title=Science, Religion and Deep Time|chapter=Chapter 9 THE TIES THAT BIND: Death and Eternity|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UdZ2EAAAQBAJ&dq=eternity+etymology+death&pg=RA1-PT68|publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]]|edition=1|isbn=9781000522945|doi=10.4324/9781003256656-10|quote=our relationship to eternity, our response to death and endings, and lessons for living are all related to the theme that will be our focus here}}</ref>

==Etymology==
[[Cicero]] used the word aeternitatis, in the work: [[De Inventione]] 1, 27, 39.,<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Henry|last1=Liddell|author-link1=Henry George Liddell|first2=Robert |last2=Scott |author-link2=Robert Scott (philologist)|last3=Jones|first3=Henry |author-link3=Henry Stuart Jones |editor=Spiros Doikas|title=aeternus|url=https://lsj.gr/wiki/aeternus|access-date=10 February 2023|website=[[A Greek–English Lexicon|Liddell, Scott, Jones Ancient Greek Lexicon]]|date=1940|via=merriam-webster.com/dictionary/eternity|quote=Tempus est pars quaedam aeternitatis, Cic. Inv. 1, 27, 39}}</ref>{{efn|tempus autem est—id quo nunc utimur, nam ipsum quidem generaliter definire difficile est—pars quaedam aeternitatis cum alicuius annui, menstrui, diurni nocturnive spatii certa significatione.<ref>{{cite book|author=M. Tullius Cicero|editor=Eduard Stroebel|chapter=Cic. Inv. 1.39|chapter-url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2008.01.0683%3Abook%3D1%3Asection%3D39|title=Rhetorici libri duo qui vocantur de inventione|publisher=Aedibus [[B. G. Teubner|B.G. Teubneri]]: [[perseus.tufts.edu]] republication|location=[[Lipsiae]] 1915: republished by the Department of Classical Studies, [[Tufts University]]}}</ref>}} written at some time between the years 88 - 81 BC<ref>{{cite book|author=James D. Williams|editor=James D. Williams|date=4 May 2009|chapter=Part II: Classical Roman Rhetoric 7 Cicero and the Latinization of Greek Rhetoric|title=An Introduction to Classical Rhetoric Essential Readings|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5WmSiNotw8QC&dq=DE+INVENTIONE+CICERO&pg=PA319|page=319|isbn=9781405158602|publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]]|quote=Cicero wrote De Inventione in his youth, although the exact date of composition is uncertain, with most scholars suggesting it was produced sometime between 88 and 81 BC.}}</ref> which is an early or the earliest extant written form from which the English word is derived;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/eternity|title=eternity noun Word History Etymology|publisher=[[Merriam-Webster]] (an [[Encyclopaedia Britannica]] company)|quote=[[Middle English]] eternite, from Middle French eternité, from Latin aeternitat-, aeternitas, from aeternus}}</ref> first shown in history in a ''[[:wikt:circa|circa]]'' 1374 translation by [[Chaucer]].<ref>{{cite web|author=[[Oxford English Dictionary]]|url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/eternity_n?tl=true|title=eternity noun Factsheet|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref> The first usage in French is 1175: eternitez: [[:fr:Benoît de Sainte-Maure|B. de Ste-Maure]], within ''[[Benoît de_Sainte-Maure#Chronique des ducs de Normandie|'ducs de Normandie]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnrtl.fr/etymologie/%C3%A9ternit%C3%A9|title=Éternité, subst. fem.|author=[[Centre national de ressources textuelles et lexicales]]|date=2012|publisher=www.cnrtl.fr|access-date=December 28, 2025|archive-date=February 23, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223020626/http://www.cnrtl.fr/etymologie/%C3%A9ternit%C3%A9|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Philosophy ==
{{see also|Eternalism (philosophy of time)|Philosophical presentism|Philosophy of space and time}}

===Eastern tradition===
In [[traditional Chinese]] 永 (''yǒng'' 'eternity') exists in the 論語 (''[[Analects]]''). <ref>{{cite web|author=Ministry of Education|author-link=Ministry of Education (Taiwan)|language=zh|url=https://dict.revised.moe.edu.tw/dictView.jsp?ID=11914&q=1&word=%E6%B0%B8|title=永|website=moe.edu.tw|location=[[Taipei]]|publisher=National Academy for Educational Research|quote=《論語．堯曰》：「四海困窮，天祿永終}}</ref>

===Western tradition===

====Classical====
The concept of eternity formed in ancient philosophy was specifically from within the [[Platonic tradition]]. <ref>{{cite web|author=А. А. Зайцев|url=https://www.pravenc.ru/text/158324.html|title=ВЕЧНОСТЬ|publisher=pravenc.ru Церковно-научный центр «[[Православная Энциклопедия]]»|language=ru|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103164126/https://www.pravenc.ru/text/158324.html|archive-date=3 January 2026|quote=Понятие В. в главных чертах было сформировано в античной философии. - наиболее полное развитие получило в платонической традиции (''Plat''. Tim.; ''Plot''. Enn. III 7. 1-4; ''Procl''. In Tim. 11)}}</ref> During the [[Classical antiquity|Classical period]] (8th-7th century BC{{efn|In [[the Iliad]] attributed to [[Homer]] (c. 8th century BC) [[List of Greek deities#Major deities in Greek religion|the gods]] are ἀθάνατος <ref name="Lorenzo">{{cite book |last=Garcia Jr |first=Lorenzo |title=Homeric Durability: Telling Time in the Iliad. |publisher=[[Harvard University]] [[Washington, DC]]: [[Center for Hellenic Studies]]. |series=Hellenic Studies Series 58 |chapter=1. Immortal and ageless forever? The spatial and temporal dimensions of immortality |chapter-url=https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/5-the-impermanence-of-the-permanent-the-death-of-the-gods/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421145520/https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/5-the-impermanence-of-the-permanent-the-death-of-the-gods/|archive-date=21 April 2021}}</ref> ([[Immortality|ἀθανασία]]<ref>{{cite web |title=ἀθανασία |url=https://lsj.gr/wiki/%E1%BC%80%CE%B8%CE%B1%CE%BD%CE%B1%CF%83%CE%AF%CE%B1 |website=[[LSJ]]}}</ref>) καὶ ἀγήρως <ref name=Lorenzo/> (appearance physically never any older through time)}} - 473/529 AD){{efn|Termination of the classical era: the last [[Western Roman Emperor]] (473), <ref>{{cite web|author=[[Ministry of National Education (Poland)|Ministerstwa Edukacji Narodowej]]|url=https://zpe.gov.pl/a/when-and-where-did-classical-antiquity-begin/D3IqPwdgL|title=when and where did classical antiquity begin?|website=zpe.gov.pl|publisher=[[Poland#Government and politics|gov.pl]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260516142024/https://zpe.gov.pl/a/when-and-where-did-classical-antiquity-begin/D3IqPwdgL|archive-date=16 May 2026|quote=the collapse of the Western Roman Empire in 473 CE. - Classical antiquity is the period in the culture of Greece and Rome from around the ninth century BC (the times of Homer) until the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the fifth century CE}}</ref> the last [[Platonic Academy]] in [[Athens]] ends (529), <ref>{{cite book |last=Hadas |first=Moses|author-link=Moses Hadas|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dOht3609JOMC&q=%22end+of+antiquity%22&pg=PA273|chapter=Chapter 16 Literature of Religion |title=A History of Greek Literature |date=1985 |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |isbn=0-231-01767-7 |page=273 |orig-date=1950|quote=Philosophy continued to be taught in Athens until the schools were closed by Justinian in 529. This gesture has been correctly taken to mark the end of antiquity}}</ref> }} [[Plato]] (c. 428–423 BC - 348/347 BC) described time as ''a moving image of eternity''<ref>{{cite book|last=de Callataÿ|first=Godefroid|date=July 2016|editor=Yitzhak Y. Melamed|location=Institut Orientaliste de Louvain, [[UCLouvain]]|chapter=Reflection: Eternity and World-Cycles|chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/book/3176/chapter-abstract/144061495?redirectedFrom=fulltext&login=false|title=Eternity: A History|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199781874.001.0001|ISBN=9780199345175|publisher=[[Oxford Academic]]-[[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref>{{efn|:37d
:[[:s:el:Τίμαιος#p37d|Τίμαιος]]

{{quote|When the father creator saw the creature which he had made moving and living, the created image of the eternal gods, he rejoiced, and in his joy determined to make the copy still more like the original; and as this was eternal, he sought to make the universe eternal, so far as might be. Now the nature of the ideal being was everlasting, but to bestow this attribute in its fulness upon a creature was impossible. Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eternity itself rests in unity; and this image we call time.|[[:s:Timaeus (Jowett)|translated in 1871]]}}

{{quote|the Living Being that is for ever existent, he sought to make this universe also like it, so far as might be, in that respect. on the generated thing. But he took thought to make, as it were, a moving likeness of eternity; and, at the same time that he ordered the Heaven, he made, of eternity that abides in unity, an everlasting likeness moving according to number—that to which we have given the name Time.|translated in 1937<ref>{{cite book|author=Silvia De Bianchi|location=[[Università degli Studi di Milano]]|editor1= Daniel Vázquez|editor2=Alberto Ross|date=Feb 2022|chapter-url=https://brill.com/display/book/9789004504691/BP000007.xml#R000292|chapter=Chapter 6 Eternity, Instantaneity, and Temporality Tackling the Problem of Time in Plato’s Cosmology 6.1 Introduction: Can Time Arise from Durationless Atemporality?|title=Time and Cosmology in Plato and the Platonic Tradition|publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]]|series=Brill's Plato Studies Series|volume=9|doi=10.1163/9789004504691_008|ISBN=9789004504691|quote=Timaeus 37d1–5<sup>6</sup> 6. }} (in [[Timaeus (dialogue)|Timaeus]] [[:s:Timaeus|37]]<ref name="Smith16526">{{cite book |last=Smith |first=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QdzrNQG3D2YC&q=Aristotle+Physics+8.6+eternity+of+the+universe |title=The Cambridge Companion to Plotinus |date=13 August 1996 |publisher=[[Cambridge University]] |isbn=0521476763 |editor-last=Gerson |editor-first=Lloyd|editor-link=Lloyd P. Gerson|page=197 |chapter=8 Eternity and Time |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QdzrNQG3D2YC&dq=Aristotle+Physics+8.6+eternity+of+the+universe&pg=PA196|quote=Plato's definition of time as the "moving image of eternity" (''Timaeus'' 37d6--7)}}</ref> [[:s:el:Τίμαιος#p37d|D]]<ref name="Smith16526" /><ref>{{cite web |author=納富信留 (''Noburu Notomi'')|author-link=:ja:納富信留|date=12 August 2018|location=[[University of Tokyo]]|title=Plato on Time and Eternity: Timaeus 37C-38C |url=https://jsns.jp/wp/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/12.11_Summaries.pdf |website=jsns.jp |publisher=新プラトン主義協会 (Japanese Society for Neoplatonic Studies)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028091729/https://jsns.jp/wp/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/12.11_Summaries.pdf|archive-date=28 October 2021}}</ref>) using the word: [[:wikt:αἰών|αἰών]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Robert Parker |title=Oxford Classical Dictionary |date=7 March 2016 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |chapter=Aion: Extract |doi=10.1093/acrefore/9780199381135.013.227 |quote=In early Greek αἰών means...'whole lifetime'...perhaps through application to the kosmos, the lifetime of which is never-ending, that the word acquired the sense of eternity (cf. Pl. Ti. 37d; Arist. Cael. 279a23–8) |chapter-url=https://oxfordre.com/classics/display/10.1093/acrefore/9780199381135.001.0001/acrefore-9780199381135-e-227}}</ref> Plato stated the [[Cosmos|kosmos]] was ἁγἡρων (ageless) in Timaeus 33a, <ref>{{cite book|author=Andrea Nightingale|author-link=Andrea Nightingale |location=[[Stanford University]]|date=May 2021|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Philosophy_and_Religion_in_Plato_s_Dialo/-XAjEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Plato+he+ordered+the+heavens+to+eternity&pg=PA253&printsec=frontcover|chapter=5.7 Earthly and Divine Time|title= Philosophy and Religion in Plato's Dialogues|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|page=253|ISBN=9781108837309}}</ref> in 37e6–38a6 the [[Theory of forms|eternal forms]] are contrasted with the [[temporality]] of the world. {{sfnp|Deng|2018|loc=§. 3.2, "[https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/eternity/#SourAnti The {{lang|la|Sources in Antiquity}}]"}} [[Aristotle]] (384–322 BC) stated [[:wikt:οὐρανοῦ|οὐρανοῦ]] was eternal (in [[:s:el:Περί Ουρανού|Book I]] of [[De caelo|Περὶ οὐρανοῦ]])<ref>{{cite journal |author=Maria Varlamova |date=2018 |title=Philoponus on the Nature of the Heavens and the Movement of Elements in Against Aristotle on the Eternity of the World |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/328295451 |journal=Scrinium: Revue de patrologie, d'hagiographie critique et d'histoire ecclésiastique |location=[[Saint Petersburg State University of Aerospace Instrumentation]] |publisher=[[BRILL]] |volume=14 |issue=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Aristotle |url=https://classicalliberalarts.com/wp-content/uploads/ARISTOTLE_DE_CAELO.pdf |title=De Caelo |publisher=[[Humphrey Milford]] 1922 |location=[[St John's College, Oxford University]] |page=279, lines 25-28, footnote |translator1=J. L. Stocks |chapter=Book I. 9 |quote=On the same principle the fulfilment of the whole heaven, the fulfilment which includes all time and infinity, is 'duration' a name based upon the fact that it is ''always'' <sup>1</sup> duration immortal and divine. <sup>1</sup> αἰών is derived from άεἰ ὢν. (Preface textual notes - [[Karl von Prantl|Prantl]] taken as basis.) |translator2=H. B. Wallis |translator1-link=John Leofric Stocks |via=Robert Parker (2016) Oxford Classical Dictionary doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780199381135.013.227}}</ref> and an [[Eternity of the world|eternal world]] (in ''[[Physics (Aristotle)|Physics]]'').<ref>{{cite web |title=Eternity of the World |url=https://www.theology.ox.ac.uk/boundsci/eternity-world |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181208120859/https://www.theology.ox.ac.uk/boundsci/eternity-world |archive-date=8 December 2018 |website=Faculty of Theology and Religion |publisher=[[University of Oxford]]}}</ref> 

The ancient Greek word for everlastingness was ἀίδιος (''aidios'')<ref>{{cite book |author=Giannis Stamatellos |title=ODIP Online Dictionary of Intercultural Philosophy |date=May 2020 |publisher=[[Institute of Philosophy & Technology]] |editor=Thorsten Botz-Bornstein |chapter=Aion (αἰών) |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342048922}}</ref> as exists via [[Plotinus]], who also used the word ''aoin'' <ref>{{cite book |author1=J.R.G. |author1-link=James Robinson Graves |title=A Discussion on the Doctrine of Endless Punishment Between Rev. J.R. Graves, D. D., L. L. D., Editor of "The Baptist," Memphis Tenn. and Rev. John C. Burruss, Editor of the "Universalist Herald" Notasulga Ala. |author2=J.C.B. |date=1880 |publisher=J.O. Perkins & Co. |publication-place=Atlanta, Ga. |page=136 |chapter=Letter VIII |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QR3SP6UA9zUC&dq=Aion&pg=PA136}}</ref> (eternity), in [[Enneads|Ennead]] III.7. <ref>{{cite work |author=Giannis Stamatellos |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325721879 |title=Eternity in Plotinus: Abstract |date=December 2013 |publisher=DEREE-[[The American College of Greece|Αμερικανικό Κολλέγιο Ελλάδος]] |location=[[Athens]] |via=Giannis Stamatellos (2007) Plotinus and the Presocratics: A Philosophical Study of Presocratic Influences in Plotinus' Enneads: "Plotinus’ central discussion on eternity (αἰών) and time (χρóνος) appears in Ennead III.7, On Eternity and Time." SUNY Press}}</ref>

====17th century====
[[Thomas Hobbes]] was re-stating the sense of the definition of [[Boethius]] when <ref>{{cite book|author=Yitzhak Y. Melamed|author-link=Yitzhak Melamed|editor=Yitzhak Y. Melamed|location=[[Johns Hopkins University]]|chapter=Chapter 3 Eternity in Early Modern Phiosophy|title=Eternity a History|chapter-url=https://philarchive.org/archive/MELETH|publisher=New York: [[Oxford University Press USA]]|publication-date=July 2016|page=129|series=Oxford Philosophical Concepts|ISBN=9780199781867}}</ref> published 1662, as a response to [[John Wallis]],<ref>{{cite book|author=James Loxley|location=[[University of Edinburgh]]|editor=Philip Major|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Literatures_of_Exile_in_the_English_Revo/oQD1xOwpwJEC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Mr.+Hobbes+Considered+in+his+Loyalty,++1662++Dr.+John+Wallis.&pg=PA148&printsec=frontcover|chapter='Not Sure of Safety': Hobbes and Exile|title=Literatures of Exile in the English Revolution and Its Aftermath, 1640-1690|publisher=[[Ashgate Publishing|Ashgate]]|publication-date=2010|page=148|series=Transculturalisms 1400-1700: Series II|ISBN=1409476146}}</ref> he wrote that he considered that "eternity is a permanent now".<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hobbes |first1=Thomas |author-link=Thomas Hobbes |title=M<sup>r</sup> Hobbes considered in his Loyalty, Religion, Reputation, and Manners. By way of Letter to D<sup>r</sup> Wallis|url=https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=RtsqMwEACAAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false|page=50|publisher=[[Andrew Crooke and William Cooke|Andrew Crooke]], the sign of the Green-Dragon in [[Saint Paul's]] Churchyard, [[London]]|year=1662}}</ref>

====19th century====
In post [[French Revolution|revolution]] France, <ref>{{cite book|author=Mike Rapport|location=[[University of Glasgow]], [[Scotland]]|editor=Randall D. Law|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_Routledge_History_of_Terrorism/3ZCsBwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Louis+Auguste+Blanqui+the+reign+of+terror&pg=PA71&printsec=frontcover|chapter=The French Revolution and Early European Revolutionary Terrorism|title=The Routledge History of Terrorism|publisher=[[Routledge]] [[Taylor & Francis Group]]|orig-date=2015|publication-date=2015|page=63, 71|ISBN=1317514874}}</ref> [[revolutionary]] <ref>{{cite magazine|author=W.J. Fishman|author-link=William J. Fishman|url=https://www.historytoday.com/archive/louis-auguste-blanqui-stormbird-revolution|title=Louis Auguste Blanqui: Stormbird of Revolution|magazine=[[History Today]]|volume=14|issue=6 June 1964}}</ref> [[Louis Auguste Blanqui]] {{efn|his politics, that were: "a revolutionary voluntarism - sometimes led Blanqui to failure - nevertheless saved him from the straitjacket [''marais gluant''] of 'scientific' [[determinism]]."<ref>{{cite book|author1=Daniel Bensaïd|author2=Michael Löwy|editor1=Philippe Corcuff|editor2=Alain Maillard|chapter-url=https://www.radicalphilosophyarchive.com/article/auguste-blanqui-heretical-communist/#ref-22|chapter=Auguste Blanqui, heretical communist - Auguste Blanqui, prophetic communist and regulated anarchist|title=Les Socialismes français à l’épreuve du pouvoir|publisher=[[:fr:Éditions Textuel|Textuel]], Paris|orig-date=2006|publication-date=2014|via=[[Radical Philosophy]] archive, Series 1, 1972-2014, issue RP 185, May/Jun 2014, translated by Philippe Le Goff}}</ref>}} wrote his 1872 cosmological [[prison literature]] <ref>{{cite journal|last=Pendakis|first=A|url=https://criticalinquiry.uchicago.edu/andrew_pendakis_reviews_eternity_by_the_stars/|title=Andrew Pendakis reviews Eternity by the Stars|publication-date=19 January 2016|journal=[[Critical Inquiry]]|publisher=[[uchicago.edu]]}}</ref> hypothesis ''L'Éternité par les astres'', <ref>{{cite web|author=Guillaume Delaunay|date=20 December 2022|language=fr|url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/accueil/fr/html/auguste-blanqui-leternite-par-les-astres|title=Auguste Blanqui, L’éternité par les astres|publisher=[[Bibliothèque nationale de France|BnF Gallica]]}}</ref> while imprisoned in Fort du Taureau [[sea fortress]]. <ref>{{cite web|author=Frank Chouraqui|date=2026|location=[[Leiden University]]|url=https://cup.columbia.edu/book/eternity-by-the-stars/9781971559353/|title=Eternity By the Stars New Edition Louis-Auguste Blanqui. Translated and Introduction by Frank Chouraqui Eris|publisher=[[Columbia University Press]]|orig-date=July 2026}}</ref>

== Physics ==
{{See also|Chronology of the universe}}

[[Camille Flammarion]] (1893) described eternalness as being [[:wikt:absolute#Adjective|the absolute]]. <ref>{{cite magazine|author=Camille Flammarion|author-link=Camille Flammarion|title=The End Of Our World|url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Scientific_American/ja9RfZeyVrkC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Eternity+by+the+Stars&pg=PA14737&printsec=frontcover|magazine=[[Scientific American Supplement]]|volume=XXXVI|number=922|publication-date=1893|publisher=[[Munn and Co.]]|page=14737|quote=We do not comprehend or conceive of infinite space and time, because we are incapable of it. But this incapacity does not invalidate the existence of the absolute}}</ref>

In 1983; [[Paul Steinhardt|Steinhardt]] proposed [[eternal inflation]], the first of two models based on [[Alan Guth|Guth]]'s [[inflationary model]] <ref name=Guth>{{cite book|author=Guth A|author-link=Alan Guth|editor=E. P. S. Shellard|editor2=G. W. Gibbons|editor-link2=Gary Gibbons|editor3=S. J. Rankin
|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_Future_of_Theoretical_Physics_and_Co/yLy4b61rfPwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=eternal+inflation&pg=PA740&printsec=frontcover|chapter=Chapter 40 Inflation and cosmological pertubations|title=The Future of Theoretical Physics and Cosmology Celebrating Stephen Hawking's 60th birthday|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|orig-date=2003|publication-date=2003|ISBN=0521820812}}</ref> of 1981 (originating with Староби́нский (''[[Alexei Starobinsky|Starobinsky]]'') 1979)<ref>{{cite symposium|author=Linde A|author-link=Andrei Linde|editor=Claes Fransson|editor2=Lars Bergstrom|editor-link2=Lars Bergström (physicist)|editor3=Per Carlson|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Particle_Physics_And_The_Universe/S0TVCgAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=old+inflation&pg=PA168&printsec=frontcover|chapter=Inflationary Cosmology|journal=[[Physica Scripta]]|volume=T85, 2000|publication-date=1999|title=Particle Physics And The Universe, Proceedings Of Nobel Symposium 109|publisher=[[The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]. [[World Scientific Publishing Company]]|ISBN=9814492140}}</ref> of the so-called [[big bang theory]] for the explanation of the orign of the universe; <ref>{{cite web|author=Linde A|author-link=Andrei Linde|url=https://web.stanford.edu/~alinde/|title=Inflationary Multiverse|publisher=[[Stanford University]] Department of Physics}}</ref> the second model [[chaotic inflation]] <ref name=Guth/> (1983) -  ''eternal chaotic inflation'' (1986), was proposed by Линде (''[[Andrei Linde|Linde]]'') <ref>{{cite magazine|author=Scott Shackelford|url=https://stanfordmag.org/contents/worlds-without-end|title=Features Worlds Without End Marrying particle physics (the study of the very small) to cosmology (the study of the very large), Andrei Linde argues that our universe is just one of many.|magazine=[[Stanford Magazine]] November/December 2007|publisher=[[Stanford University]]|quote=His theory of “eternal chaotic inflation” followed in 1986. “Instead of a universe with a single law of physics, eternal chaotic inflation predicts a self-reproducing, eternally existing multiverse where all possibilities can be realized,” Linde says.}}</ref> 

The possibility of eternal universes with reference to [[General Relativity]] was a subject of physics since the 21st century.<ref>{{cite work|author1=Damien A. Easson|author2=Joseph E. Lesnefsky|date=2 May 2024|url=https://arxiv.org/html/2404.03016v1|title=Eternal Universes|arxiv=2404.03016v1}}</ref>

== Poetry ==
The ''[[kanji]]'' for eternity is used in the Japanese ''[[Manyōshū]]''. <ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.co.uk/books?redir_esc=y&id=GfAPAAAAYAAJ&focus=searchwithinvolume&q=eternity|title=The Manyōshū: The Nippon Gakujutsu Shinkōksi Translation of One Thousand Poems, with the Texts in Romaj|translator=Nihon Gakujutsu Shinkokai|translator-link=Japan Society for the Promotion of Science|publisher=[[Columbia University Press]], 1965|page=187, 312}}</ref> The comments in ''[[The Rape of Lucrece]]'' by [[William Shakespeare]] 
{{quote|
:Who buys a minute's mirth to wail a week? 
:Or sells eternity to get a toy?}} are in a poem based on the work of [[Ovid]] and [[Livy]] of the history of [[Ancient Rome]] particularly the [[Lucretia#Rape|rape of Lucretia]] by [[Sextus Tarquinius|Tarquin]]. <ref>{{cite web|author=Lynne Hunt|url=https://www.enotes.com/topics/rape-lucrece/questions/need-know-which-play-that-has-this-shakespeare-184731|title=The Rape of Lucrece by William Shakespeare |publisher=[[enotes.com, Inc.]]|via=- A concordance to Shakespeare's poems; an index to every word therein contained [[Horace_Howard_Furness#Personal|Mrs. Horace Howard Furness]], [[J.B. Lippincott & Company]] 1875, p.86}}</ref>

== Religion ==
Eternity as infinite duration is an important concept in many lives and [[religion]]s. [[God]] or gods are often said to endure eternally, or exist for all time, forever, without beginning or end. Religious views of an [[afterlife]] may speak of it in terms of eternity or [[Immortality|eternal life]].{{efn|For examples: {{harvp|Bassali|2008|p=138}}, quote: "In the next life, there will be two places only - heaven and hell. {{omission}} In heaven, you will spend an eternity of bliss, light, and glory with God. In hell, you will spend an eternity of woe, darkness and torment apart from God. Which of these two places would you prefer to spend your eternity?"}}

===Abrahamic religions===
{{see also|Alpha and Omega|Eternity of God in Christianity|Unto the ages of ages}}
In [[Book of Genesis|Genesis]] 21:33 of the [[Old Testament]]<ref name=JCJ>{{cite web|author=John C. Jeske| url=http://essays.wisluthsem.org:8080/bitstream/handle/123456789/2371/JeskeForever.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y|title=Exegetical Brief: םלוֹע־דע"Forever"|publisher=[[Wisconsin Lutheran Seminary]]|quote=in the Old Testament. םלוֹע־ is used to describe God's person. Genesis 21:33 calls him םלוֹע־לא, "the eternal God."}}</ref> El-Olam<ref name=OUH2016>{{cite journal|author=Oleh Uwe Hummel|title=NAMA ALLAH: DIMULIAKAN ATAU DIPERALAT?|url=https://stt-gke.ac.id/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Volume-6-Nomor-1-Juni-2016.pdf|journal=PAMBELUM: Jurnal Teologi Kontekstual|volume=6|number=1|date=June 2016|location=[[:id:Sekolah Tinggi Teologi Gereja Kalimantan Evangelis|Sekolah Tinggi Teologi Gereja Kalimantan Evangelis]]|publisher=stt-gke.ac.id|language=id|page=9|quote=El –Olam: Nama םל וֹע לאberarti “Allah yang Kekal”. Olam sebenarnya berarti jagad raya (universe) atau kekekalan (eternity). El Olam identik dengan “TUHAN” (הוהי), yaitu Allah yang disembah oleh para leluhur Israel di Bersyeba (lihat Kej. 21:33; Maz. 90:1-3; Yes.26:4). }}</ref> is God-Eternal.<ref name=JCJ/><ref name=OUH2016/><ref>{{cite book|author=Brian Ogren|editor=Brian Ogren|title=Time and Eternity in Jewish Mysticism: That Which is Before and That Which is After|chapter=Introduction: That Which is Before [And That Which is After]|publisher=[[BRILL]]|date=27 January 2015|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BPxyBgAAQBAJ&dq=olam+eternity&pg=PR5|volume=48 of Studies in Jewish History and Culture|page=4|isbn=978-9004290310}}</ref>

[[Jesus]] In [[the Gospels]] explicitly threatens ''the wicked'' with an eternal punishment.<ref>{{cite web|author=Maria Pia Ciccarese|location=[[La Sapienza]]|language=it|url=https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/inferno_(Enciclopedia-dei-ragazzi)/|title=Inferno — L'inferno cristiano|publication-date=2005|quote=Nel Vangelo Gesù minaccia esplicitamente il castigo eterno per i malvagi. }}</ref> In the context of [[Book of Revelation|Revelation]] 14: 9-11 of [[the Bible]], the book Revelation describes how smoke from application of [[Sulfur#Toxicity of sulfur compounds|burning sulphur]] onto those who ''worship [[The Beast (Revelation)|the beast]]'' will transit upwardly forever. <ref>{{cite book|author1="Iōánnēs" (''John of [[Patmos]]'' / ''unknown'')|author2=C. Stephen Layman|author-link2=C. Stephen Layman|title=C. Stephen Layman: Is the Bible the Word of God? An Essay on the Authority of the Bible & [[The Holy Bible English Standard Version]], 2001|chapter=Chapter 21 The Problem of Hell |publisher=[[Wipf and Stock Publishers]] & [[Good News Publishers]] |publication-date=November 2025|ISBN=9798385260089|page=(no page number shown)}}</ref> The position onto which sinners are condemned for all time into [[hell]], if the souls are punished in a conscious state of existence, is known as [[traditionalism]],  and [[annihilationism]] if the punishment on arrival in the infernal dominion is that their consciousness is then annulled-extincted.  <ref>{{cite web|author=Robert A. Peterson|location=[[Covenant Seminary]]|orig-date=May 31, 2012|publication-date=Jan 26, 2026
|url=https://www.equip.org/articles/the-dark-side-of-eternity-hell-as-eternal-conscious-punishment/|title=The Dark Side of Eternity: Hell as Eternal Conscious Punishment ''Truth matters, Life matters more''|publisher=[[The Christian Research Institute]]}}</ref> [[Thomas Aquinas]] (c. 1225 – 1274) believed in an eternal God, without either a beginning or end; the concept of eternity is of [[divine simplicity]], thus incapable of being defined or fully understood by humankind.{{sfnp|Helm|2010|loc=§. 6, "[https://stanford.library.sydney.edu.au/archives/sum2010/entries/eternity/#:~:text=Medieval%20thinkers,-It%20is%20in&text=For%20Aquinas%20God%27s%20eternity%20is,fully%20grasped%20by%20a%20creature. Medieval thinkers]"}} Christian theologians may regard [[immutability (theology)|immutability]], like the eternal [[Platonic realism|Platonic form]]s, as essential to eternity.{{sfnp|Deng|2018|loc=§. 3.1, "[https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/eternity/#LociClas The {{lang|la|Loci Classici}}]"}}{{efn|{{harvp|Deng|2018}}, quote: "Augustine connects God's timeless eternity to God's being the cause of all times and God's immutability."}}

In the [[Islam]]ic context, while ''[[:wikt:أزل|azal]]'' indicates eternity at the beginning of known time and ''[[:wikt:أبد#Etymology_1.3|abad]]'' at the end; ''[[sarmad]]'' indicates all (both) aspects,<ref>{{cite book|last=Nasr|author-link=Seyyed Hossein Nasr|first=Seyyed|location=[[George Washington University]]|date=1989|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Knowledge_and_the_Sacred/IChnJl0Mu4sC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=azal+and+abad&pg=PA247&printsec=frontcover|chapter=Chapter 9 Principle knowledge and the Multiplicity of Sacred forms|title=Knowledge and the Sacred|publisher=[[State University of New York Press]], [[Albany, New York|Albany]]|page=247|ISBN=9780791401767}}</ref> this latter as an [[adjective|adjectival]] form is in ''[[surah]]'' 28 parts 71 and 72 of the [[Qur'an]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Mohamed Haj Yousef|location=[[United Arab Emirates University]]|date=April 2014|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Ibn_Arab%C3%AE_Time_and_Cosmology/wDx8AgAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=azal+and+abad&pg=PT97&printsec=frontcover|chapter=2.20 Other expressions of time|title=Ibn ‘Arabî - Time and Cosmology|publisher=[[Routledge]]|series=Culture and Civilization in the Middle East|ISBN=0-203-93824-0|doi=10.4324/9780203938249|quote=It is most widely used as an adjective, ''sarmadî'', meaning everlasting, and this is how it is used in a very pertinent discussion of time in the Qur'an (28:71-72)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://legacy.quran.com/28/71-77|title=Surat Al-Qaşaş (The Stories) - سورة القصص|publisher=quran.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260514134518/https://legacy.quran.com/28/71-77|archive-date=14 May 2026}}</ref> In Islamic culture the eternity of the universe was a subject in the writings of ''[[Abu Ali ibn Sīna]]''<ref name=Dilek>{{cite book|author=Selman Dilek|location=[[Ibn Haldun University]]|editor=Reza Hajatpour|publication-date=November 2025|chapter=The Philosophical Nature of Mystical Knowledge Ibn al-Arabi's Examination of the Debate on the Eternity of the World in the Islamic Intellectual Tradition|chapter-url=https://books.google.co.uk/books?hl=en&lr=&id=yMudEQAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PA153&dq=Kitab+al-Azal++Eternity&ots=KLnCkLZvbr&sig=asYJtIfw_HFMAoI46nrmphZPo90&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false|page=154|title=Philosophy and Mysticism in the Islamic World|publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG]]|series=Philosophy in the Islamic World in Context|volume=5|ISBN=3112218205|quote=figures - actively engaged in the discourse of the universe's eternity - (1037), Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1111), Abu Walid Muhammad Ibn Rushd (1198)|via=iask.ai/q/ancient-persian-word-eternity-ir1hhc8}}</ref> (died 1037), <ref>{{cite web|author=Nader El-Bizri|author-link=Nader El-Bizri|location=|url=https://www.iis.ac.uk/scholarly-contributions/ibn-sina-or-avicenna/|title=Ibn Sina or Avicenna|website=iis.ac.uk|publisher=[[The Institute of Ismaili Studies]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250415210947/https://www.iis.ac.uk/scholarly-contributions/ibn-sina-or-avicenna/|archive-date=15 April 2025|via=Dilek 2025 (''[[ibid]]'')}}</ref> ''[[Abu Hamid al-Ghazali]]'', ''[[Abu Walid Muhammad Ibn Rushd]]''.<ref name=Dilek/>

===Egyptian===
Ancient Egyptian eternity terms were neheh, for cyclical time, and djet, for linear.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Michael Stausberg|title=Approaches to the Study of 'Time' in the History of Religions|date=2004 |journal=Temenos: Nordic Journal for the Study of Religion|volume=40|issn=2342-7256|doi=10.33356/temenos.4829|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite work|author=Steven R. W. Gregory|date=February 2022|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/358469547|title=Tutankhamun Knew the Names of the Two Great Gods: Dt and nHH as Fundamental Concepts of Pharaonic Ideology.|publisher=[[Archaeopress]]|page=1, 5|doi=10.2307/j.ctv2b07tzx|isbn=9781789699852|quote=the ancient Egyptian terms ''dt'' and ''nhh'', each of which, from the manner in which they have usually been interpreted in Egyptological scholarship, has been thought to denote infinite time}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=D. A. Ziborova|location=V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/360901779|title=Time-Eternity: Ancient Egyptian Temporal Concept in the Context of Ancient Greek Philosophy|journal=UDC|volume=94|issue=32|page=79|quote=ancient Egyptians temporal categories: nHH (neheh) and Dt (djet) and their comparison with the tradition of ancient Greek philosophy. It is shown that these terms can be defined as time-eternity. Attention is focused on the definition of the term nHH as associated with the solar god and the cyclic movement, innite duration of recovery and cyclic length, and term Dt as the eternity associated with Osiris, the other world of the dead, imperishableness, constancy and “eternal sameness”.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Janice Kamrin|date=1 February 2017|url=https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/telling-time-in-ancient-egypt|title=Timeline of Art History Telling Time in Ancient Egypt|location=1000 [[Fifth Avenue]] New York|publisher=[[The Metropolitan Museum of Art]]|quote=two kinds of eternity. Linear time, or djet, associated with the funerary god Osiris, had a beginning and would have an end, albeit in the infinitely far future. Neheh, cyclical time, was tied to the passage of the sun through the sky during the day and the Netherworld during the night. Ideally, an Egyptian who had lived according to the precepts of maat by supporting and maintaining the proper order of a just cosmos, and who had been accorded a proper burial, would live forever (djet) and ever (neheh).|access-date=December 29, 2025|archive-date=January 15, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260115002811/https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/telling-time-in-ancient-egypt|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Willeke Wendrich|date=2013|editor1=Alain Schnapp|editor2=with: Lothar von Falkenhausen|editor3=Peter N. Miller|editor4=Tim Murray|chapter=ANTIQUARIANISM IN EGYPT THE IMPORTANCE OF ''RE''|title=World Antiquarianism Comparative Perspectives|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0skBAAAQBAJ&dq=djet+eternity&pg=PA142|publisher=[[Getty Research Institute]], [[Los Angeles]]|page=142|isbn=978-1-60606-148-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Claude Traunecker|author-link=Claude Traunecker|date=2001|title=Les Dieux de L'Egypte|chapter=Chapter 3 The Gods and their Universe DIVINE SPACE AND TIME|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y78zDGDCUjkC&dq=djet+neheh&pg=PA37|edition=1|language=en|translator=David Lorton|page=37, Divine Time|publisher=[[Cornell University Press]]|isbn=9780801438349}}</ref> [[Rameses III]]<ref name=FA2007>{{cite book|author=Farid Atiya|date=2007|title=The Pocket Book of Ancient Egypt|chapter=Medinet Habu|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LyWNFVeblO8C&dq=temple+of+Ramses+III+United+with+Eternity&pg=PA352
|publisher=[[American University in Cairo Press]]|page=332|isbn=9789771744399}}</ref> (c.1187-1156 B.C.E.) <ref>{{cite web|url=https://preview.memphis.edu/egypt/resources/colortour/westbank6.php|title=Thebes - Temple of Ramesses III|location=[[Tennessee|TN]]|publisher=[[The University of Memphis]]}}</ref> [[funerary temple]]<ref name=FA2007/> was: 'United-with -Eternity'.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Harold H. Nelson|title=The Identity of Amon-Re of United-with-Eternity|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/542124|journal=[[Journal of Near Eastern Studies]]|volume=1|number=2|date=April 1942|pages=127–155 |publisher=[[The University of Chicago Press]]: [[ITHAKA]]|doi=10.1086/370633 |jstor=542124 |via=[[William J. Murnane]] (1980) isac.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/uploads/shared/docs/united.pdf [[Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures|OI]] & [[American University in Cairo Press|AUCP]]}}</ref>

===Greco-Roman===
[[Greek_mythology#Sources|Mythic]]<ref name=DG>{{cite book|author=Dante L. Germino|date=1982|
title=Political Philosophy and the Open Society|chapter=Chapter III The Open Society and the Birth of Philosophy|chapter-url=
https://books.google.com/books?id=zjOIXqrcjkYC&dq=%E1%BC%80%CE%B8%CE%AC%CE%BD%CE%B1%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%82+(athanatos)&pg=PA74|page=74, The Pre-Socratic Philosophers and the Break with Myth|location=[[University of Virginia]]|publisher=[[Louisiana State University Press]] - [[Baton Rouge]] & [[London]]|isbn=9780807109748}}</ref> [[Iliad]]ical<ref>{{cite book|author=Homer|author-link=Homer|editor=Walter Leaf|editor-link=Walter Leaf|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iKJfAAAAMAAJ&dq=%E1%BC%80%CE%B8%CE%AC%CE%BD%CE%B1%CF%84%CE%BF%CF%82+Iliad&pg=PA80|title=The Iliad|chapter=IΛIΑΔΟΣ Ξ (xiv.)|date=1888 |location=[[Trinity College, Cambridge]]|publisher=[[Macmillan Publishers|Macmillan]], 1888|page=80|quote=Ξάνθου δινἡεντος, ôν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς}}</ref><ref name=LSJἀθάνατος>{{Cite web|first1=Henry|last1=Liddell|author-link1=Henry George Liddell|first2=Robert |last2=Scott |author-link2=Robert Scott (philologist)|last3=Jones|first3=Henry |author-link3=Henry Stuart Jones |editor=Spiros Doikas|title=ἀθάνατος|url=https://lsj.gr/wiki/ἀθάνατος|access-date=31 December 2025|website=[[A Greek–English Lexicon|Liddell, Scott, Jones Ancient Greek Lexicon]]|date=1940}}</ref> [[:wikt:ἀθάνατος|ἀθάνατος]] (athanatos) is the [[Immortality|immortal]].<ref name=DG/> 

The ancient greek word for everlasting, and/or eternal, exists in the [[Orphica Hymni]].<ref>{{Cite web|first1=Henry|last1=Liddell|author-link1=Henry George Liddell|first2=Robert |last2=Scott |author-link2=Robert Scott (philologist)|last3=Jones|first3=Henry |author-link3=Henry Stuart Jones |editor=Spiros Doikas|title=ἀΐδιος|url=https://lsj.gr/wiki/%E1%BC%80%CE%90%CE%B4%CE%B9%CE%BF%CF%82|website=[[A Greek–English Lexicon|Liddell, Scott, Jones Ancient Greek Lexicon]]|date=1940|quote=English (LSJ) [ᾱῐδ], ον, also η, ον, Orph.H.10.21}} - {{cite book|editor=Carola Schenkl|editor2=Eugenius Abel|url=https://archive.org/details/orphicaaccedunt00abelgoog/mode/2up|title=Orphica|date=1885|publisher=[[Lipsiae]]: G. Freytag Pragae: F. Tempsky}}</ref>

The timelessness in [[divinity]] of classical period [[Augustine]] (354–430 AD), as exists in [[:s:Confessions (Augustine)|Book XI]] of [[the Confessions]], and [[Boethius]] (c. 480–524), in [[:s:The Consolation of Philosophy (James)/Free Will and God's Foreknowledge|Book V]] of [[the Consolation of Philosophy]] were adopted as the reality of the subject for later thinkers in the [[Western philosophy|western tradition of philosophy]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Deng |first=Natalja |editor2=Uri Nodelman |title=Eternity The ''loci classici'' |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2007/entries/eternity/ |website=[[The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]] (Spring 2025 Edition) |quote=(Following the work of Boethius and Augustine)" [of [[Thagaste]]] "(divine timelessness became the dominant view.)...what came to be the dominant account of eternity in western philosophy and theology|editor1=Edward N. Zalta}}</ref> Boethius stated eternity was: ''interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio'',<ref name=MB2014>{{cite journal|author=Margherita Belli|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44211274|title=The Fortune of Boethius's Concept of Eternity in the Scholastic Debate|journal=Carmina Philosophiae|volume=23|issue=Special Issue: The Medieval Legacy of Boethius on the Continent|date=2014|pages=31–60 |publisher=International Boethius Society: [[ITHAKA]] |jstor=44211274 }}</ref> which is translated as "simultaneously full and perfect possession of interminable life".{{sfnp|Boedder|1902|loc=book 2, ch. 2, "[https://maritain.nd.edu/jmc/etext/nath34.htm The Eternity of God]"}}{{efn|{{harvp|Boethius|523|loc=book 5, prose §. 6}}, quote: "{{lang|la|Aeternitas igitur est interminabilis uitae tota simul et perfecta possessio}}"}} and ''nunc permanens'', which in English is a: permanent now.<ref name=MB2014/> 

===Vedic===
Within the [[Historical Vedic religion|Vedic]] <ref>{{cite book|author1=Namrata R. Mahanta|location=[[Banaras Hindu University]], [[Uttar Pradesh]]|author2=Banibrata Mahanta|editor1=R.N. Rai|editor2=M.S. Pandey|editor3=Anita Singh|chapter=Chapter 3 The Nation As Goddess:Ritualizing Politics, Politicizing the Sacral|chapter-url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Theory_and_Praxis/KA7nBwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Rigveda,+Aditi&pg=PA45&printsec=frontcover|title=Theory and Praxis: Indian and Western|publisher=[[Cambridge Scholars Publishing]]|date=2015|ISBN=1443876828}}</ref> [[Rigveda]], [[Aditi]], as a goddess, is eternal. <ref>{{cite web|url=https://jansankalp.org/docs/trinity/origins-of-gods/aditi/|title=Aditi|publisher=Jansankalp Foundation}}</ref>

===Graphic art===
Some of the works of [[MC Escher]] were explorations of the idea of eternity.<ref>{{cite web|author2=Escher, MC|author1=Erik Kersten|author2-link=MC Escher|orig-date=1958|publication-date=1 March 2017|url=https://escherinhetpaleis.nl/en/about-escher/escher-today/path-of-life-i|title=Path of Life I|publisher=[[Escher in The Palace]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Erik Kersten|author2=Escher MC|author2-link=MC Escher|author3=Penrose R|author3-link=Roger Penrose|publication-date=18 March 2018|orig-date=March 1960|url=https://escherinhetpaleis.nl/en/about-escher/escher-today/ascending-and-descending|title=Ascending and Descending|publisher=[[Escher in The Palace]]}}</ref>

===Symbolism===
Eternity is often symbolized by the endless snake, swallowing its own tail, the [[ouroboros]].<ref>Origen, ''[[Contra_Celsum]]'' 6.25.</ref> The circle, band, or ring is also commonly used as a symbol for eternity, as is the mathematical [[symbol of infinity]], <math>\infty</math>. Symbolically, these are reminders that eternity has no beginning or end.
